name: Aaron
source_summary: Moses' older brother and spokesman before Pharaoh, consecrated as Israel's first high priest at Sinai; built the golden calf in Moses' absence, and died on Mount Hor after his priestly garments were transferred to his son Eleazar.
family_friendly_summary: Aaron was Moses' older brother, and God chose him to speak for Moses because Moses didn't feel confident speaking in public. Aaron stood beside Moses through many of the amazing miracles that convinced Pharaoh to let God's people go free. Later, Aaron became Israel's very first high priest, with special clothes and a special job of representing the people before God. But Aaron also made a big mistake — while Moses was away, Aaron gave in to pressure and helped the people build a golden calf to worship instead of God. Even after that, God still used Aaron in his priestly role for the rest of his life. Aaron's story shows that even important, God-chosen leaders can give in to pressure sometimes, but God can still keep using them afterward.
adult_story: Aaron, three years older than Moses, is introduced at the burning bush as God's answer to Moses' objection he could not speak well: God appointed Aaron as Moses' mouthpiece before Pharaoh and Israel (Exodus 4:10-16, 27-31). Aaron performed several signs himself, including turning his staff into a serpent and bringing on the plagues of blood, frogs, and gnats (Exodus 7:8-12, 19-20; 8:5-6, 16-17). At Sinai, Aaron and his sons were set apart as Israel's first priests, and Aaron alone was consecrated high priest, permitted into the Holy of Holies once a year to atone for the nation (Exodus 28-29; Leviticus 16). Scripture does not soften what came next: with Moses forty days on the mountain, the people demanded gods to lead them, and Aaron collected their gold, cast a calf, and proclaimed a feast to the LORD — a violation of the covenant by the man who would become high priest (Exodus 32:1-6). Moses' intercession, not Aaron's merit, turned aside the wrath (Exodus 32:9-14, 30-35). Aaron's authority was tested again when he and Miriam challenged Moses' standing, for which Miriam alone was struck with leprosy while Aaron pleaded for her healing (Numbers 12). When Korah rose against Aaron's priesthood, God vindicated him by making his staff alone, of twelve gathered, sprout, bud, and bear almonds overnight (Numbers 16-17). Aaron died on Mount Hor at 123, his garments transferred to his son Eleazar (Numbers 20:22-29). Hebrews treats Aaron's priesthood as real but temporary, pointing forward to Christ's permanent priesthood (Hebrews 7:23-28).
devotionals: Aaron’s story teaches us about priesthood; may we look to Jesus, whose grace and truth never fail.
Through Aaron’s experience of mediation, God teaches us to trust His wisdom and follow Jesus faithfully.
